title: Scrotal Abscess -- Introduction
content: A scrotal abscess is a localized collection of purulent material in the wall of the scrotum, involving the skin and subcutaneous tissues. The scrotum is a pendulous sac composed of skin, dartos muscle, and multiple fascial layers, including the external spermatic cord, cremasteric muscle and fascia, internal spermatic cord, and tunica vaginalis. Each hemiscrotum contains the testis, epididymis, and spermatic cord. The rich vascular supply and loose connective tissue of the scrotum predispose the area to rapid spread of infection.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Introduction
content: Scrotal abscesses typically develop following bacterial inoculation, skin infections, or extension from deeper adjacent infections. Predisposing factors include diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, poor hygiene, tobacco use, advanced age, alcohol use disorder, obesity, renal failure, atherosclerosis, and malnutrition. [1] Scrotal abscesses are distinct from other intrascrotal pathologies, which can be differentiated by ultrasonography. [2] [3]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Introduction
content: The natural history of a scrotal abscess is characterized by an acute inflammatory response with pain, swelling, and erythema that develops over several days, culminating in the accumulation of purulent material. Diagnosis is typically based on the patient's history and physical examination, and management typically consists of surgical incision and drainage. Clinicians should be vigilant for potential complications, including sepsis and the life-threatening necrotizing infection known as Fournier gangrene. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Fournier Gangrene ," for further information.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Etiology
content: Scrotal abscesses typically develop due to a local bacterial infection of the scrotal skin or subcutaneous tissues following minor skin trauma (eg, shaving) or folliculitis. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism. [4] The local immune response in scrotal abscess formation involves significant neutrophil recruitment, leading to enzymatic tissue digestion and the formation of an abscess cavity. [5] [6] [7] [8]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Etiology
content: In some cases, scrotal abscesses may develop after a deeper perineal infection, most commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes and anaerobic bacteria. Rarely, remote intra-abdominal processes, such as ruptured appendicitis, pancreatitis, or bowel perforation, may lead to scrotal abscess development. [9] [10] [11] [12] [13] [14] [15] Please see StatPearls' companion resources, " Fournier Gangrene " and " Streptococcus Pyogenes ," for further information.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Etiology
content: Tuberculous scrotal abscesses are quite rare in the United States; however, globally, they account for 3% to 7% of all extrapulmonary tuberculosis cases, particularly in regions with higher tuberculosis prevalence, including parts of Africa, China, and India. [16]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Etiology
content: In children, scrotal abscesses may be associated with epididymo-orchitis, undiagnosed and untreated testicular torsion, spread of an intra-abdominal infectious process through a patent processus vaginalis, a hematogenously spread infection, ejaculatory duct dysfunction, caudal obstruction of the Wolffian duct, vesicoureteral reflux, or ectopic ureteral insertion into the posterior urethra. [5] [17] [18] [19] [20] [21]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Epidemiology
content: Precise epidemiological data on isolated scrotal abscesses are currently unavailable. These conditions are often managed in the outpatient or emergency settings and often coded under general skin and soft tissue infections; therefore, site-specific data are lacking. Results from a large retrospective cohort study in the United States reported an incidence of 496 skin and soft tissue infections per 10,000 person-years, with abscesses accounting for a significant proportion of cases. Although this study did not report anatomical or site-specific data, it provides a useful estimate of the burden of abscess-related infections in the general population. [4] More recent data, however, suggest that the rise of skin and soft tissue infections in the early 2000s has plateaued and may be declining. [22] [23] [24]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Epidemiology
content: Risk factors for scrotal abscess formation are similar to those for subcutaneous abscesses at other skin sites. Common risk factors include diabetes mellitus, immunosuppressive states, obesity, poor personal hygiene, chronic kidney disease, smoking, injection drug use, long-term Foley catheter use, history of scrotal trauma or urogenital surgery, urinary tract or perineal infections, epididymo-orchitis, sexually transmitted diseases, HIV, alcohol use disorder, advanced age, and various underlying dermatological conditions, such as hidranenitis suppuriativa. [5] [25] [26] [27] [28] [29] [30] Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Hidradenitis Suppurativa ," for further information.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Epidemiology
content: The use of sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors has recently emerged as a potential risk factor for Fournier gangrene. [31] These medications inhibit the sodium glucose cotransporter in the proximal renal tubules. [32] This cotransporter uses the intracellular sodium gradient generated by the sodium-potassium adenosine triphosphatase pump to reabsorb glucose from the urine into the bloodstream. [32] Inhibition of SGLT2 reduces glucose reabsorption, leading to significant glucosuria. [32] These medications have only rarely been linked to Fournier gangrene, but the United States Food and Drug Administration and the European Medicines Agency have released a box warning regarding this possible association. [31] [33] [34] [35] [36] [37] [38] The association is not definitive because diabetes mellitus is also a risk factor for Fournier gangrene, and findings from recent reviews have not confirmed a causal relationship. [1] [34] [38] [39] [40]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Pathophysiology
content: The skin is the body's first line of defense against microbial invasion, providing both a physical barrier and an immunological shield against invading pathogens. Scrotal abscesses may form when scrotal skin is disrupted, allowing bacteria to enter the subcutaneous tissue. This infection triggers a local acute inflammatory response, involving activation of the innate immune system and the accumulation of neutrophils at the site of infection. Neutrophils release enzymes and reactive oxygen species to destroy invading organisms, causing liquefactive necrosis and local tissue damage. [5] [6] [7] [8] This accumulation of neutrophils, bacteria, and cellular debris forms the purulent material within the abscess cavity. [5] [6] [7] [41] [42]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Histopathology
content: Microscopically, subcutaneous abscesses show features of acute suppurative inflammation, with a cavity filled with purulent material composed of neutrophils, bacteria, necrotic cellular debris, and exudate. The surrounding subcutaneous tissue may be edematous and demonstrate infiltration with inflammatory cells, predominantly phagocytic cells. In chronic abscesses, granulation tissue and fibroblast proliferation occur, leading to fibrosis and scarring. [5] In scrotal wall abscesses, inflammatory changes are typically confined to the subcutaneous tissues and dermis, with no involvement of the epididymis, testis, or other intrascrotal structures. [5]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- History and Physical
content: Obtaining a detailed history and performing a thorough physical examination are often sufficient to diagnose a scrotal abscess. Patients typically present with a painful, tender scrotum with localized swelling that develops over several days. Patients may also present with fever or systemic symptoms, suggesting possible sepsis.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- History and Physical
content: On physical examination, a superficial, palpable mass is identified within the scrotal wall. This mass is usually tender, fluctuant, with surrounding erythema, warmth, or features of cellulitis. If the abscess has ruptured, purulent material may exude from the wound. The underlying testis and epididymis are typically nontender and anatomically normal, distinguishing scrotal abscess from other intrascrotal pathologies. Red flags suggesting complications include the following: Crepitus on palpation Gas in the abscess cavity on ultrasonography Necrotic skin Rapid progression of infection Severe systemic illness, fever, or sepsis

title: Scrotal Abscess -- History and Physical
content: Scrotal pyoceles are rare infectious disorders of the scrotum. [43] These disorders often present as a collection of purulent fluid in the hydrocele space surrounding the testicle, and are typically associated with a scrotal infection or epididymo-orchitis. [43] [44] Clinical symptoms include subacute scrotal pain, edema, and erythema. [43]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- History and Physical
content: Scrotal pyoceles can be differentiated from hydroceles by their clinical symptoms and ultrasonographic findings, including air-fluid levels and abnormal internal echoes within the hydrocele sac, which indicate loculations, debris, and septations. [43] [45] [46] [47] Treatment involves broad-spectrum antibiotics and surgical drainage; however, many cases ultimately require an orchiectomy. [43] [44] [48] If left untreated, this condition may progress to Fournier gangrene. If Fournier gangrene is a consideration, a computed tomography scan is recommended to better define the extent and margins of the infection. [43] [49] Please see the companion StatPearls' resource, " Fournier Gangrene ," for further information.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Evaluation
content: The diagnosis is primarily clinical; however, it may be supported by imaging (scrotal ultrasonography) and laboratory testing. Routine clinical assessments include oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, and temperature. Blood testing is not routinely required; however, if diagnostic uncertainty persists, a complete blood count and C-reactive protein level may be helpful. In patients who are systemically unwell or have features of sepsis, a more comprehensive panel of blood tests should be performed, including renal and liver function tests, a coagulation profile, blood gas analysis, lactate and glucose levels, and blood cultures.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Evaluation
content: A hemoglobin A1c level may be considered to screen for undiagnosed diabetes mellitus. Urinalysis may be performed at the bedside to help exclude a urinary tract infection because results are typically normal in an isolated scrotal abscess.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Evaluation
content: Scrotal ultrasonography helps distinguish an abscess from other scrotal masses and testicular pathologies. [50] [51] [52] [53] Typical sonographic features of a scrotal abscess include an avascular localized hypoechoic or complex fluid collection with posterior acoustic enhancement within the scrotal wall, often with septations and debris, usually surrounded by soft-tissue edema or cellulitis, producing a cobblestone appearance. [50] [51] [52] [53] [54] [55] [56]

[50] [51] [52] [53] [54] [55] [56]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Evaluation
content: Doppler vascular flow color imaging demonstrates an avascular area corresponding to the abscess cavity with a surrounding area of markedly increased vascularity corresponding to adjacent inflammation and cellulitis. [5] [50] [51] The presence of gas within the abscess is an ominous sign and is characteristic of Fournier gangrene. [57] Magnetic resonance imaging may also be used; however, ultrasonography is preferred initially due to its low cost, availability, and quickness. [58] [59]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Treatment / Management -- Antibiotic Selection
content: Incision and drainage remain the definitive treatment for most scrotal and other subcutaneous abscesses, but empirical antibiotic treatment is frequently administered in tandem, or, in rare cases, in isolation. [60] [61] [62] [63] [64] Antibiotics alone, along with warm compresses or hot sitz baths, can sometimes be used as definitive management for very small collections without overlying cutaneous infection or systemic features, and for patients who are not suitable candidates for surgical management. [60] [64] Sitz baths may also be used postoperatively to promote wound cleansing. The most recent guidelines from the Infectious Diseases Society of America, updated in 2014, recommend adjunctive antibiotics targeting S aureus when systemic features of infection are present. [60] Targeted antibiotics based on cultures and sensitivity results should be used for recurrent abscesses. [60]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Treatment / Management -- Antibiotic Selection
content: Results from a systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 randomized controlled trials involving 4198 patients found that antibiotics significantly reduce the risk of treatment failure, hospitalization, and recurrence; however, their use is associated with increased gastrointestinal adverse effects. [65] Findings from another meta-analysis of 4 studies involving 2406 patients supported this, highlighting a higher rate of clinical cure with antibiotics compared with placebo. [66]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Treatment / Management -- Antibiotic Selection
content: Culture results are frequently unobtainable, infrequently alter clinical management or initial antibiotic selection, and may be unnecessary without demonstrable impact on patient outcomes. [67] [68] [69] [70] [71] Although this may be true in simple, uncomplicated cases with small (<2 cm) lesions in otherwise healthy adults, a study found that culture results directly led to changes in therapy in 65% of patients, particularly in those with high-risk factors. [27]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Treatment / Management -- Antibiotic Selection
content: A wound culture is still recommended because the results may help guide antibiotic selection in complex or recalcitrant cases with prolonged cellulitis, in patients with diabetes mellitus or immunocompromise, in patients at the extremes of age, or when systemic symptoms are present. Cultures are also advisable for recurrent and large abscesses (>5 cm), infections from human or animal bites, antibiotic resistance, and epidemiological tracking. [60] [72] [73] [74] [75] [76] [77] Overall, antibiotics appear beneficial for reducing recurrent abscess formation and improving outcomes, regardless of abscess size, causative organism, comorbidities, or systemic signs. [62] [63] [65] [66] [78] [79]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Treatment / Management -- Antibiotic Selection
content: Aspiration of purulent material for culture before incision of the abscess is superior to a specimen obtained after the abscess is opened due to a lower risk of bacterial contamination. [77] [80] The overlying skin of the abscess should first be properly disinfected, and a large-bore needle should be used for aspiration. A Gram stain is also recommended because it provides more rapid information about the infecting organism than culture, which requires 24 to 48 hours to yield results.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Treatment / Management -- Antibiotic Selection
content: Antibiotic use and selection should be considered on an individual basis, taking into account each patient's clinical condition, site and severity of the infection, presence of systemic disease, comorbidities, drug excretion and metabolism, renal and liver function, mode of administration, adverse effects, local antibiotic resistance patterns, medication allergies, most likely causitive pathogens, likelihood of progression, and risk of complications. [81] [82] [83] [84]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Treatment / Management -- Antibiotic Selection
content: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) can provide a rapid (<2 hours) and reliable indication of MRSA presence in the abscess. [85] [86] With an outstanding negative predictive value of >98%, the test can reliably rule out MRSA, thereby avoiding the use of inappropriate and unnecessary anti-MRSA antibiotics. [87] [88] [89] [90]  PCR testing detects bacterial DNA, which is present even in nonviable microorganisms; therefore, it can be used even after antibiotic administration. [91] However, PCR testing provides no information on antibiotic sensitivities and has a low positive predictive value. [87] [89] [92] [93] Nevertheless, it can be very helpful in selecting initial antibiotic therapy and should be used where available.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Treatment / Management -- Commonly Used Antibiotics for Scrotal Abscesses
content: Empiric antibiotic therapy for scrotal abscesses may include cefazolin, piperacillin-tazobactam, clindamycin, imipenem, vancomycin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and tetracyclines, such as doxycycline and minocycline, which are often used in combination. [94]  Mild infections may be treated with oral antibiotics, whereas more severe abscesses require parenteral therapy.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Treatment / Management -- Commonly Used Antibiotics for Scrotal Abscesses
content: Most strains of S aureus are now methicillin-resistant, making penicillin derivatives ineffective. Effective antibiotics include oral doxycycline (100 mg twice daily), minocycline (200 mg initial dose, then 100 mg daily), trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (1 or 2 double-strength tablets twice daily), and intravenous (IV) tigecycline (100 mg IV initial dose, then 50 mg twice daily). [95] [96] [97] [98] Please see StatPearls' companion resources, " Trimethoprim Sulfamethoxazole ," " Doxycycline Hyclate ," and " Minocycline ," for further information.

Effective antibiotics include oral doxycycline (100 mg twice daily), minocycline (200 mg initial dose, then 100 mg daily), trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (1 or 2 double-strength tablets twice daily), and intravenous (IV) tigecycline (100 mg IV initial dose, then 50 mg twice daily). title: Scrotal Abscess -- Treatment / Management
content: Indications for parenteral antibiotic therapy: Indications are based on the severity and extent of the abscess, as well as patient factors and comorbidities. Hospital admission is typically required to ensure appropriate preoperative administration. These indications include the following: Evidence of immunocompromise (current or recent administration of cancer chemotherapy or immunosuppressive drugs, neutropenia, HIV, and frequent opportunistic infections) Inability to swallow or absorb oral antibiotics Large abscess or extensive surrounding cellulitis Rapid progression of infection Systemic signs of infection (fever >38 °C, hypotension, and tachycardia)

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Management
content: Incision and drainage is the standard recommended treatment for subcutaneous and scrotal abscesses. Initial management of scrotal abscesses should ensure adequate pain relief and prevention of complications. In most cases, this includes the appropriate use of antibiotics based on clinical judgement, antibiograms, infection severity, patient factors, and local protocols. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Incision and Drainage ," for further information.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Management
content: Incision and drainage may be performed under local or general anesthesia, with the choice of anesthesia typically influenced by the abscess depth and severity, clinical factors, surgical judgment, and patient preferences. [107] [108] Advantages of local anesthesia include avoiding hospital admissions, fewer inpatient days, improved operating room efficiency, shorter delays in definitive treatment, faster return to normal activities, and reduced overall costs. [61] However, local anesthesia is less effective in infected tissue due to the low pH, which reduces the percentage of the more active, uncharged form of the anesthetic. [109] [110] Please see StatPearls' companion resource, " Incision and Drainage ," for further information.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Management
content: Large abscesses (>5 cm), anatomical abnormalities, closely adjacent vasculature, equivocal or atypical ultrasonography findings, or unusually complex lesions are best treated surgically. [111] [112] When performed under general anesthesia, appropriate preoperative preparation and coordination with the anesthesiologist and interprofessional teams are essential to ensure patient safety and procedural efficiency. In such cases, preoperative antibiotics should be administered.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Management
content: In an appropriately anesthetized patient, an incision is made with a scalpel over the area of greatest fluctuance. Purulent material is expressed, and curettage is performed to remove loculations and necrotic, infected tissue. Extensive irrigation with sterile saline is performed, followed by irrigation with an antiseptic solution, such as 0.05% chlorhexidine gluconate (preferred) or 1% betadine. [113] [114] Hemostasis via diathermy may be required in some cases. Depending on the size of the abscess cavity, it may be packed with a hydrofiber dressing to maintain hemostasis. The wound is left open to heal by secondary intention, preventing premature skin closure before the infection is fully eradicated and avoiding an empty subcutaneous cavity. [113]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Management
content: An alternative surgical procedure to conventional incision and drainage for subcutaneous abscesses is loop drainage. [81] In this method, 2 small incisions are made at opposite poles of the abscess, loculations are removed, and a vessel loop is inserted through the incisions to allow continuous drainage of the cavity. [81] [115] Needle aspiration is a less invasive technique for abscess drainage, but it is generally not recommended due to its high failure rate. [81] [116] However, needle aspiration is considered the optimal method for obtaining a pus sample for Gram staining and culture. [77] [80] [116]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnosis of scrotal abscess includes a broad range of conditions that may present with a scrotal swelling, tenderness, or erythema, including: Epididymal cyst Epidermoid neoplasm Epididymo-orchitis Folliculitis Fournier gangrene Granuloma Hematoma Hydrocele Inguinal hernia Lymphoma Pyocele Ruptured appendicitis Scrotal pustule Scrotal pyocele Sebaceous cyst Spermatocele Testicular abscess Testicular torsion Testicular tumor or neoplasm Torsed appendix testis (hydatid of Morgagni) Varicocele

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Prognosis
content: With early diagnosis and appropriate management, scrotal abscesses have an excellent prognosis. In otherwise healthy individuals, most cases resolve without significant complications. However, delays to treatment or factors known to impair wound healing, such as diabetes mellitus, immunosuppression, tobacco smoking, corticosteroid use, or obesity, may delay recovery time or increase the risk of progression to systemic infection or other complications. The recurrence of scrotal abscesses should prompt evaluation for underlying predisposing conditions.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Complications
content: Most scrotal abscesses resolve with appropriate surgical management. However, if left untreated or inadequately managed, they may progress to a range of local and systemic complications. Potential complications include the following: Cellulitis Extension into the deeper scrotal and perineal tissues Failure to resolve (refractory) Fistula formation Progression to Fournier gangrene, a life-threatening form of necrotizing fasciitis Prolonged healing time Recurrence Scarring Sinus tract formation

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Complications
content: Timely and appropriate medical management is essential to reduce the risk of these complications. However, abscesses recur in approximately 10% of cases, even with incision and drainage and a complete course of antibiotics. [62] [63] Reasons for this include the following: Bacterial resistance to the chosen antibiotic, especially for MRSA. When the culture and sensitivity results are available, the antibiotic choice should be optimized Incomplete antibiotic treatment duration Fistula formation Inadequate abscess drainage or loculations (identified with ultrasonography and repeat wound exploration) Incorrect or inadequate antibiotic dosage Misdiagnosis Presence of a foreign body Undiagnosed comorbid conditions such as HIV, immunosuppression, and diabetes mellitus

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care -- Postoperative Care
content: Following incision and drainage of scrotal abscesses, postoperative care should focus on promoting wound healing, patient comfort, preventing recurrence, and monitoring for complications. As the wound is typically left open to heal by secondary intention, patients should be instructed in wound care and in monitoring for signs of complications. [117] Depending on the type of packing and the goals (hemostasis in the immediate postoperative period versus maintaining an open cavity to promote healing by secondary intention), appropriate nursing follow-up for wound review and packing changes should be considered. [118]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care -- Postoperative Care
content: Analgesia should be optimized to minimize postoperative discomfort, particularly during dressing changes. Vacuum-assisted closure dressings should be considered. [119] [120] [121] [122] Scrotal supports may reduce swelling and alleviate postoperative discomfort after various scrotal procedures. The utility of repeated packing in subcutaneous abscesses is controversial. Recent studies have questioned the benefits of repeated packing, suggesting it may lead to worse outcomes, increased pain, and prolonged healing times. [123]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care -- Vacuum-Assisted Wound Care
content: Vacuum-assisted wound care is effective for treating scrotal abscesses, particularly for large abscesses or after debridement for more severe infections. [124] [125] Vacuum therapy for wounds promotes faster healing by removing excess exudate, preventing fluid accumulation, increasing blood flow, facilitating management of large defects, reducing hospitalization days, promoting granulation tissue growth, and minimizing the need for frequent dressing changes. [119] [120] [121] [122] [124] [125] [126] [127] However, achieving adequate positioning and air seal can be challenging in this anatomical region. The use of skin adhesives, surgical gloves, vacuum-assisted closure dressings, and vacuum-assisted closure baskets can be beneficial. [121] [128] [129] [130] [131]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care -- Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy
content: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy may be considered postoperatively as an adjunctive treatment in more severe or recalcitrant infection with significant cellulitis. In early Fournier gangrene, hyperbaric oxygen therapy enhances the effects of antibiotics, reduces inflammation, increases blood flow, eliminates anaerobic bacteria, and promotes healing. [132] [133] [134]

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Consultations
content: Patients presenting with scrotal abscesses may be treated initially by primary care or emergency clinicians. Definitive management typically involves consultation with a urologist or, in some cases, a general surgeon to perform and oversee the surgical treatment. Additional specialist involvement may include radiologists and ultrasonography technicians, who perform and interpret diagnostic imaging such as ultrasonography. Anesthesiologists are involved in the care of patients who have incision and drainage performed under anesthesia. Infectious disease specialists may help with antibiotic selection. Plastic surgeons and wound care specialists may help with postoperative care. Nurses are integral to the management and aftercare of abscesses, particularly regarding wound care and cavity packing. Patients with hidradenitis suppurativa may benefit from a dermatological assessment, although severe disease may require consultation with plastic or general surgery.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Effective prevention of scrotal abscesses relies on managing modifiable risk factors and improving awareness of early symptoms. Patients should be educated and encouraged to maintain good personal hygiene, including regular bathing of the genital area to reduce the risk of bacterial colonization and skin breakdown. Men should use genital protection during sports. For patients with diabetes mellitus, improving glycemic control may reduce the risk of skin and soft-tissue infections and improve wound healing. Smoking cessation should be encouraged, as it may reduce the incidence of complications and improve wound healing.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Key preventive measures include keeping the scrotal area clean and dry; using condoms; staying up to date with all recommended vaccines, such as mumps; avoiding scrotal skin trauma from shaving or waxing; and maintaining good urinary Foley catheter care. Regular testicular self-examinations also help identify issues early.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Warning patients to be vigilant for signs of worsening infection postoperatively is important to ensure early detection of complications and facilitate timely care. Education should include monitoring for increasing pain, erythema, swelling, discharge, and systemic signs such as fever, rigors, or malaise. Clear guidance should be provided to patients on when and how to seek medical attention to reduce the risk of serious complications.

title: Scrotal Abscess -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Effective management of scrotal abscesses relies on a coordinated, patient-centric, interprofessional approach to minimize pain and distress and optimize outcomes.
